open_obligations: Check whether verifier-leading Stackelberg equilibria can be found with Chen et al.'s oracle-based algorithms.
Note the shift from regret minimisation to Stackelberg leadership.
Note that Theorem 8 is stated only for problems that have a valid proof system.
in.other_title: Theorem 8: for problems with a valid proof system, valid interactive proofs = approximate verifier-leading Stackelberg equilibria of nip
in.rationale: Chen et al. propose games with very large action spaces as a model for language games and AI debate, and ask for notions of equilibrium better suited to these games. Hammond and Adam-Day prove that, for a probabilistic decision problem that has a valid proof system, a profile is a valid interactive proof system iff it is an approximate verifier-leading Stackelberg equilibrium of a nip game, while noting worst-case losses and Stackelberg equilibria are hard to learn. The cited passages do not show that nip games are language games or AI debate games with very large action spaces, so Theorem 8 is not shown to answer Chen et al.'s call, and Chen et al.'s call does not bear on Theorem 8; neither bears on the other's claim.
in.scope: proposed SHARES_TOPIC: notions of equilibrium for games used as formal models of AI debate or interactive proofs; the cited passages do not show that nip games are games with very large action spaces of the kind Chen et al. study

text: The authors propose games with very large action spaces as a formal model for language games and AI debate, calling it only a starting point. They pose further directions: different oracle models for best response, other notions of regret, and notions of equilibria better suited to these games.
title: Open: oracle models, regret notions and equilibria suited to language games
